clinicalPearls: Presents in the neonatal period with profound hypotonia, feeding difficulties and often excessive sleepiness or reduced arousal
Neonatal problems can include temperature instability, hypersomnolence and apnoea or hypoventilation
A prominent movement disorder emerges, with dyskinesias, dystonia, tremor and exaggerated startle-like or myoclonic movements
Epilepsy and abnormal EEG activity are common, though some paroxysmal movements are non-epileptic and can mimic seizures
Global developmental delay with intellectual disability, absent or limited speech and delayed walking is typical
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in PURA (or 5q31.3 deletions including it), usually de novo and autosomal dominant, encoding the DNA/RNA-binding protein Pur-alpha
Distinguishing true seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal movements is a recurring clinical challenge
reference.pathophysiology: PURA encodes Pur-alpha, a highly conserved DNA- and RNA-binding protein that participates in transcriptional regulation, DNA replication and the transport and translation of messenger RNA in neurons, functions essential for normal brain development and neuronal maturation. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants, usually de novo, reduce functional protein through haploinsufficiency, disrupting neuronal differentiation and synaptic function. The resulting impairment produces the neonatal hypotonia and reduced arousal, movement disorder, epilepsy and developmental delay. Because a single functional copy is insufficient, the gene is dosage-sensitive and deletions encompassing it produce the same disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital myasthenic and neuromuscular disorders causing hypotonia
Other causes of the floppy infant
additionalInvestigations: EEG, ideally with video, to distinguish seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal movements
Brain MRI, often normal or with non-specific changes
Neuromuscular and metabolic workup for the hypotonic infant
Chromosomal microarray to detect 5q31.3 deletions involving PURA
Gene panel or exome sequencing including PURA
redFlags: Apnoea, hypoventilation or respiratory instability in the neonate
Poorly controlled seizures or status epilepticus
reference.prognosis: PURA syndrome causes lifelong moderate to severe intellectual disability with motor and often speech impairment; early neonatal risks include respiratory and feeding instability. With supportive care many children improve in arousal and feeding over infancy, and management is multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Over-treating non-epileptic paroxysmal movements as seizures
Misdiagnosing as Prader-Willi or a primary neuromuscular disorder without genetic testing
Assuming a normal MRI excludes a genetic cause
Overlooking respiratory and autonomic instability in the neonatal period
management: Control epilepsy with antiepileptic drugs, using video-EEG to distinguish true seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal movements
Manage the movement disorder of dystonia, dyskinesia and myoclonus symptomatically
Support neonatal respiratory instability, apnoea and hypoventilation with monitoring and ventilatory support as needed
Address feeding difficulties with feeding support and nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding where required
Provide developmental therapies including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy for hypotonia and global delay
Coordinate care through a neurodevelopmental multidisciplinary team
Offer genetic counselling, confirming the usually de novo variant and advising on the low recurrence risk
